title: The lamp in the theater
hookLine: a dance hall, and the lamp nobody came to watch
carry: the witness lights the whole show
tomorrow: four sayings small enough for a sticky note. what are they?
last: THE GLOW LEADS TO THE JEWEL.

lines: A DANCE, A PATRON, A CROWD.
THE LAMP IN THE EMPTY HALL.
cards: At a concert, nobody looks at the stage lights once, and nobody could see the band without them. The Panchadashi has a hall like that. A dance is on.
The patron who's paying sits up front. The audience fills the room. Musicians play, and the dancer moves.
Off to one side, a single lamp burns. Nobody came to watch it. Then the show ends, everyone goes home, and the lamp is still burning in the empty hall.

teach.b: This chapter is the Natakadipa, the lamp of the theater, and it turns the hall into a picture of a person.
The patron is the sense of I, the one who thinks the show is for him. The audience is the world of objects. The musicians are the senses.
The dancer is the mind, always moving.
And the lamp is the witness, sakshi in Sanskrit: the plain awareness that lights all of it. Watch how the lamp behaves.

teach.h: IT LIGHTS ALL OF IT, THE SAME.
teach.b: It lights the patron and the back row the same way. It doesn't prefer the dancer's best moves to her stumbles.
It doesn't leave when the music gets loud. When the hall empties, it goes on shining. The book says awareness is like that.
It lights the sense of I without being that I. It lights a busy mind and a quiet one alike. In deep sleep, when the show stops, it's still there, as the book's opening chapter said.
So the witness doesn't have to fix the performance, or stop it. Its whole job is to shine. The dancing can go on.
Knowing which one is the lamp is the lesson.

how: Hindu homes and temples keep a lamp burning during worship; Advaita teachers use the lamp as a picture of the witness that lights everything.

games.q: who's who in the hall — tap the pairs.

s: in this picture, the witness is the patron who thinks the show is for him
the patron is the sense of I. the witness is the lamp.
the lamp lights the best moves and the stumbles the same way
it lights the patron, the crowd and the dancer alike.
to find the witness, the dancing has to stop
the witness doesn't have to stop the show; it only shines.

games.q: a family wedding: loud music, two uncles arguing, a packed dance floor, and you feel pulled everywhere. what does the theater lamp suggest?
o: notice the one seeing all of it; the show doesn't have to stop.
leave; the noise is the problem, so get away from it.
join the loudest part so you're not left out of it.
games.why: the lamp doesn't fix the performance or leave when it gets loud. it lights all of it, evenly.

practice: Find one source of light where you are: a lamp, a window, a screen turned away from you. Rest your eyes near it, not on it.
See how it falls on everything in reach the same way, the tidy corner and the messy one, and let your attention be that even for the sit.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: here, the book of the theater lamp, which lights every part of the show and stays after.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the witness; here, awareness that lights everything and takes no part.

carryVoice: Pocket this: the witness lights the whole show. The lamp doesn't leave with the crowd; it's still shining when the hall is empty.

sources.ref: Panchadashi 10 (Natakadipa): the lamp in the dancing hall lights the patron, the audience and the dancer alike, and shines on when they leave; patron as ego, audience as objects, musicians as senses, dancer as intellect, lamp as the witness
